UI / UX Case Study

CuraConnect

A doctor appointment app designed to feel like a doctor you trust, not a hospital form. Online consults and in-person bookings, held in one calm flow.

Role
UI/UX Designer
Platform
iOS
Tools
Figma
Type
Telemedicine & Booking
Overview

Healthcare access,
without the friction.

Booking a doctor in most apps still feels transactional — long forms, cluttered listings, and a hard switch between "online" and "in person." CuraConnect explores a single, coherent flow that takes a user from discovering a doctor to consulting them, online or face to face, without the experience changing shape halfway through.

Problem Statement

The problem, stated plainly.

People delay seeing a doctor not because they don't care about their health, but because the apps meant to help feel like more work than the visit itself.

A short competitive look at existing booking apps surfaced the same three frictions, over and over.

FRICTION 01

Booking a routine appointment takes far more taps and screens than it should, before a user even sees a doctor.

FRICTION 02

Online video consults and in-person visits are treated as two separate products glued together, not one decision.

FRICTION 03

Doctor credibility gets reduced to a tiny thumbnail and a number — not enough to build trust before booking.

Objectives

What the design needed to do.

Four things had to be true at once for this to work as a healthcare product people actually trust.

TRUST

Feel credible on first open

Healthcare apps live or die on perceived trust. The first few screens had to feel warm and reassuring, not sterile or generic.

SPEED

Get to "booked" fast

A returning user needs the shortest possible path from "I need a doctor" to a confirmed appointment.

UNITY

One system, two visit types

Browsing and live video consults needed to share the same visual language instead of feeling like two different apps.

CLARITY

One question per screen

Each screen answers exactly one thing the user is asking in that moment — nothing more competing for attention.

Research

Who it's for.

P
Priya, 34
Marketing Manager, Hyderabad
Books care for herself and her parents

Needs

  • A fast way to find a specialist near her
  • To know a doctor is legitimate before booking
  • One place for both video and in-clinic visits

Frustrations

  • Long intake forms before she's even seen a profile
  • Switching apps for online vs. in-person care
  • Doctor listings with no rating or specialty visible

Goals

  • Book an appointment in under a minute
  • Feel confident in who she's booking, before she taps
  • Have one app for the whole family's care
Design Process

From problem to product, step by step.

A straightforward six-stage process, each stage answering one question before moving to the next.

01

Discover

Looked at how people already book doctors in apps like Practo and 1mg, and where that experience breaks down — forms before trust is established, online and offline visits split into separate flows, and doctor credibility reduced to a thumbnail and a number.

02

Define

Turned those findings into one problem statement, a single primary persona, and four non-negotiable design goals — trust, speed, unity, and clarity, all detailed above.

03

Ideate

Sketched the journey as a single line instead of a tree. Every extra branch or decision point was treated as a tax on a user who, by definition, isn't feeling their best.

04

Wireframe

Locked the information hierarchy before any color or imagery touched the screen. On Home specifically: location and search needed to sit above everything else, services needed to read in one row, and doctor cards needed their rating visible without a tap.

05

Visual Design

Applied a trust-driven palette: near-black surfaces for browsing and discovery, a warm cream interlude exactly at login, and a single teal accent carried through as the "go" color everywhere. The map below is literally the mood of each screen in the flow.

OnboardingLoginHomeVideo Call
06

Prototype & Walkthrough

Linked every screen into a clickable Figma prototype and ran informal walkthroughs with a few people outside the project. The main thing that came out of it: the swipe-to-start gesture on onboarding needed a clearer visual cue, which is why it carries a directional arrow inside the pill rather than relying on the label text alone.

Walkthrough

Four screens, one flow.

01 — Onboarding

An illustration, not a stock photo.

A friendly, illustrated doctor opens the app instead of a clinical hero shot, paired with "Quickly talk to top doctors online or in person." It signals scope (online and in-person) and lowers the emotional temperature before anything transactional begins. The swipe-to-start gesture, instead of a plain button, adds a small, intentional beat rather than rushing the user forward.

02 — Login

Proof a real doctor is on the other side.

The cartoon gives way to a photoreal doctor holding a stethoscope toward the camera — credibility, right when it's needed most. Google sign-in sits above email and password as the lower-friction default. The CTA reads "Let's login," not "Sign In," keeping the same conversational warmth from onboarding intact.

03 — Home Dashboard

Three bands, zero hunting.

Location and search sit together at the top, answering "find something near me" immediately. A single, genuinely useful promo banner sits below. "Our Services" breaks the app into four scannable categories so a specific need skips the general doctor list entirely. "Popular Doctors" surfaces specialty, location, and rating up front — the exact information needed to decide who to book, with zero taps required.

04 — Video Consultation

A familiar pattern, on purpose.

The call screen deliberately mirrors a pattern users already know, so nothing new has to be learned mid-consultation. Doctor name, credentials, and a live timer anchor the top-left; the patient's own feed sits picture-in-picture. A quiet "swipe to show chart" prompt hints at deeper functionality without cluttering the view, and the end-call button is the only thing on screen allowed to be red.

Key Features

What the flow actually does.

01

Specialty-based doctor discovery with visible ratings and location, no extra taps.

02

One booking path that doesn't fork between online and in-person visits.

03

Native video consultations with medical records reachable mid-call.

04

A services shortcut row that routes specific needs around the general doctor list.

Reflection & Next Steps

Holding four moods together.

The hardest part wasn't any single screen — it was keeping the tone consistent across very different states: a playful onboarding illustration, a trust-building login portrait, a dense functional dashboard, and a high-stakes live call. The light/dark split became the throughline that held those states together without the app feeling like four different products stitched into one.

The next stage of this process would be designing the missing "Book Doctor" step shown in the flow diagram above, plus a post-call summary screen, closing the loop between "I found a doctor" and "I have a record of what they told me."
